items.title: Marsa Gawasis (Wadi Gawasis) and the Egyptian Seafaring Expeditions to Punt
items.who: R. Fattovich and K. A. Bard
items.note: Summary of the harbour excavations, where ship timbers, cargo boxes and inscribed stelae document Middle Kingdom voyages to Punt and Bia-Punt.

items.title: Punt: Die Suche nach dem "Gottesland"
items.note: Comprehensive review of the ancient Egyptian sources and modern searches for Punt, with a full discussion of the competing locations.

items.title: Hatshepsut's expedition to the land of Punt: novelty or tradition?
items.note: Asks whether the Deir el-Bahari expedition broke new ground or continued earlier practice, which bears on how literally its scenes can be read geographically.

items.title: Punt in the 'Northern' Topographical Lists
items.note: Philological analysis of the Punt section of the New Kingdom topographical lists as a source for the placenames and peoples Egyptians associated with Punt.

items.title: Egyptian and Imported Pottery from the Red Sea port of Mersa Gawasis, Egypt
items.note: Corpus of Egyptian and foreign wares from the harbour, including southern Red Sea imports used to trace the expeditions' contacts.

items.title: Seafaring Expeditions to Punt in the Middle Kingdom: Excavations at Mersa/Wadi Gawasis, Egypt
items.who: K. A. Bard and R. Fattovich
items.note: Final synthesis of the harbour excavations and long-distance routes, favouring a Punt in the African lowlands of the southern Red Sea.

items.title: The Archaeology of Punt
items.note: Posthumously published review of the archaeological cultures of the African Red Sea hinterland proposed as Punt and their links with Egypt.

items.title: Review of Bard and Fattovich, Seafaring Expeditions to Punt in the Middle Kingdom
items.note: Review by the main proponent of an Arabian Punt, engaging the excavators' African identification.

items.title: The provenance of obsidian artefacts from the Middle Kingdom harbour of Mersa/Wadi Gawasis
items.who: G. Lucarini, D. Barca and A. Manzo
items.note: LA-ICP-MS sourcing matches harbour obsidian to both Eritrean and Yemeni sources, implying contacts with both shores of the southern Red Sea.

items.title: Toponymy on the Periphery: Placenames of the Eastern Desert, Red Sea, and South Sinai in Egyptian Documents
items.note: Systematic study of Egyptian peripheral placenames, placing Punt within a mapped Red Sea toponymy and weighing etymologies.

items.title: Mummified baboons reveal the far reach of early Egyptian mariners
items.note: Strontium and oxygen isotopes place two New Kingdom baboon mummies' birthplaces in a zone spanning Eritrea, Ethiopia, Djibouti and parts of Somalia and Yemen.

items.title: Hidden in Plain Sight, or Where to Look for the Mysterious Land of Bia-Punt
items.note: Reconsiders the location of Bia-Punt, the variant toponym recorded on Middle Kingdom monuments at Mersa/Wadi Gawasis.

items.title: From Tenochtitlán to Punt: When People Encounter the Distant and Unknown, a Cognitive Approach
items.note: Compares Hatshepsut's Punt reliefs with early modern contact accounts to ask how far encounter imagery reflects observation rather than expectation.

items.title: Adulis and the transshipment of baboons during classical antiquity
items.note: A mitogenome from a Late Period baboon mummy groups with populations of Eritrea and northeastern Sudan; the authors link this to Adulis and, more tentatively, to Punt.

items.title: Palaeopathological and demographic data reveal conditions of keeping of the ancient baboons at Gabbanat el-Qurud (Thebes, Egypt)
items.note: Pathologies and age profiles show the Theban baboons were kept and bred in captivity, which constrains how far they can source Punt.

items.title: Egyptian Geography of the Southern Red Sea: The Land of Wetenet
items.note: Distinguishes Wetenet, visited for ebony and baboons, from Punt and locates it on the Sudanese or Eritrean coast.

items.title: Esarhaddon in Yemen, Punt, and the Horn of Africa
items.venue: Journal of Ancient Near Eastern History
items.note: Locates Esarhaddon's Bāzu in South Arabia and argues that the coastal power of Pudaʾ on Wadi Zabid in Yemen was Punt.
